Pain is chronic but not acute — teams have coping mechanisms (spreadsheets, interns, part-time bookkeepers)
Depends on UNCONFIRMED hypothesis that month-end close pressure creates periodic urgency spikes; founder believes this drives willingness to switch but no confirmation
Teams do the work every month — the problem recurs, creating a persistent but low-urgency demand

assumptions_relied_on.text: Month-end close pressure creates periodic urgency spikes that drive tool switching
assumptions_relied_on.impact: If confirmed, Score 3 criterion would PASS, raising score from 2 to 3

key_signals: Pain is chronic and recurrent, not acute
No external deadline or event forcing adoption
analysis_narrative:
Urgency is the weakest dimension in this evaluation. The problem is real and recurring but not urgent — teams have learned to absorb the 6-hour weekly cost through workarounds: spreadsheets, part-time bookkeepers, or simply accepting occasional reconciliation errors. None of these workarounds are good, but they reduce the urgency to switch to something new.

The founder hypothesizes that month-end close creates urgency spikes — a plausible theory, but unconfirmed. Even if true, urgency spikes at month-end are a buying trigger, not a continuous adoption driver. B2B tools purchased to solve month-end problems often get abandoned in the intervening weeks.

This dimension scores 2 because the problem is chronic and the team will not go without a solution, but the pace of buying decisions is slow and the trigger for switching is unclear.
key_finding: Urgency is low — the problem is a chronic, managed pain rather than an acute crisis, with no external events forcing immediate resolution.
score_explanation: Score 2 reflects a recurring problem with existing workarounds that reduce the felt urgency to switch. Score 3 would require evidence that at least some teams are actively searching for solutions now, which the month-end close hypothesis might provide if confirmed.
